newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-KUERTEN FALLS ON WIMBLEDON DEBUT.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-KUERTEN FALLS ON WIMBLEDON DEBUT.

text.p: French Open champion Gustavo Kuerten stumbled out of Wimbledon at the first hurdle on Tuesday but will not be joining the growing list of clay court specialists with an allergy to grass.

Kuerten's five-set defeat to American Justin Gimelstob, ranked 117th in the world, brought to an end a glorious month in which the 20-year-old Brazilian has risen from obscurity to the fringe of the world's top 10.

But while recent French champions Sergi Bruguera and Thomas Muster, not to mention Spaniards Alex Corretja, Felix Mantilla and Albert Costa, have stayed at home rather than try their luck on grass, Kuerten will definitely be back.
"I've still things to learn but I really enjoyed it," grinned Kuerten, who has played only 10 matches on grass in his life. "I think I'll play better next time, because worse is impossible."

No one has won both Wimbledon and the French Open since Bjorn Borg retired, and Kuerten recognises the need to play a little faster, attack the net more and build up the sense of anticipation which comes with match practice.

But until he plays at Wimbledon in a year when the sun has baked the courts harder than these 1997 editions, there will be no repeat of the impromptu samba celebrations which greeted his victory in Paris.
The previous day and earlier on Tuesday, with the grass still moist and cloud cover hovering, a restless Kuerten looked as out of place as a Brazilian beachgoer on the sea-front at Clacton.
Once the sun filtered through, however, the rhythm slowly seeped back into Kuerten's game.
He reeled off two sets to square the match, outwitting the muscular Gimelstob's charges to the net with a now familiar mix of dipping forehands and deceptive passing shots.

In the end, though, without his favourite blue and yellow garb or any red Parisian clay beneath his feet, the magic touch vanished in the final set, two fatally poor volleys allowing Gimelstob to win the final set 6-4 and book a second round encounter with former champion Michael Stich.
Was it the clothes, perhaps? Wimbledon's all-white dress threats were tamely obeyed by his kit suppliers, but Kuerten himself preferred to dwell on the welcome he received from his fellow players.
"Everyone has been stopping me in the streets to say congratulations...I've said thank-you about 1,000 times," he laughed. "It's been nice but I'm looking forward to a few days off."
Before that, though, Kuerten is committed to the men's doubles with Ecuador's Nicolas Lapenti. More time on grass, more experiences to stow away for next year.
Wimbledon has not heard the last of Brazil's beach boy champion.
